question.problem:
Which of the following are orthogonal projection matrices?

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14237294/assets/13213fe5fbeaaa288ba5dadeadf50e24d8b285f4641c3291c90b45352249f8ec.svg)
question.worked_solution:
Recall that $Q$ is an orthogonal projection matrix if and only if $Q^2=Q$ and $Q^T=Q.$ 

With that in mind, let's examine our matrices.

- $A$ is *not* an orthogonal projection matrix. We have
$A^T = A$
but 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2} & =A\cdot A \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 5 \\ 5 & 10\end{aligned}] \\  & \ne A.\end{aligned}
$$

- $B$ is *not* an orthogonal projection matrix. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}{B}^{T}\ne B.\end{aligned}
$$

- $C$ is an orthogonal projection matrix. Indeed,
$C^T = C$
and

$$
\begin{aligned}{C}^{2} & =C\cdot C \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{5} & \frac{2}{5} \\ \frac{2}{5} & \frac{1}{5}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{5} & \frac{2}{5} \\ \frac{2}{5} & \frac{1}{5}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{25}[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{25}[\begin{aligned}20 & 10 \\ 10 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{5} & \frac{2}{5} \\ \frac{2}{5} & \frac{1}{5}\end{aligned}] \\  & =C.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "$C$ only."
